title: What a Gursikh does
hook: Bhai Gurdas pictures the Sikh who rises early, bathes, remembers, joins the sangat and works honestly

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat: Bhai Gurdas's roll of ordinary Sikhs, each one named. Today, the shape of their day.

What would a stranger learn about you from watching one ordinary day? Not your opinions. Just the day: what time the light went on, what you did first, where you went, how you earned your bread. Bhai Gurdas gives us the day of a Sikh who belongs to the Guru, and he doesn't describe it with a list of beliefs. He describes it with a clock. Today's word: Gursikh.
screen: `ONE ORDINARY DAY, WATCHED.` → `NOT OPINIONS, JUST THE DAY.` → `A DAY TOLD BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Gursikh puts two words together: Gur, the Guru, and Sikh. A Sikh of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas returns to this person in his vars, and the picture he paints is practical, almost a timetable. The Gursikh rises while the night is still on, in the early hours. Bathes. Then remembers: sits with the Guru's word, with the Name, before the day's noise starts. Then goes to the sangat, to sit with others and hear and sing the Guru's hymns. Then goes to work, earns a living honestly, and shares what comes in. No mountaintop, no cave: a house, a gathering, a workplace. The picture has deep roots in the Guru's own word. On Ang three hundred five of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru: rising early, bathing, meditating on the Name, and carrying the Guru's word through the rest of the day. Bhai Gurdas fills in the day around that morning. Three things stand out. First, the order. Remembering comes before the work, so the work happens inside the remembering, not instead of it. Second, the company. The Gursikh's day isn't solitary: the sangat is part of the schedule, not an extra. Third, the money. Honest work is in the picture on purpose. Holiness doesn't leave the marketplace; it walks into it with clean hands. A Gursikh, in this telling, isn't known by a title. You'd know one by watching the day.
screen: `GUR AND SIKH: A SIKH OF THE GURU.` · `RISE, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE SANGAT, THEN HONEST WORK.` · `KNOWN BY THE SHAPE OF A DAY.` · then, large: `THE GURSIKH'S DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow's first ten or fifteen minutes, a little before your usual alarm, while the house is still quiet. See what you'd do with them before the phone, wash your face, sit, breathe, read a line that matters to you, and keep it small enough to be real. If you pray, you can choose a line of the Guru's word, or say Waheguru, for that quiet.
Gursikh. A Sikh of the Guru. In Bhai Gurdas's vars, someone you'd recognize by the day: rising early, remembering, sitting in the sangat, working honestly.
Your line: the gursikh's day. Remembering first, and the work held inside it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikh custom keeps the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, for bathing and reciting or listening to the morning banis before the day's work.

rising early, bathing, and remembering the Name.

fork.reveal: Guru Ram Das (Ang 305) starts the Sikh's day early: rising, bathing, remembering the Name. Bhai Gurdas adds the sangat and honest work around it.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a Sikh of the Guru, from gur and sikh.

chat.says: What does a Gursikh's day look like, in Bhai Gurdas's picture? Mostly prayer?
options: Rising early, remembering the Name, joining the sangat, then working honestly and sharing.
Prayer all day, far from work and family, with no time spent earning money.
Earning first, and then prayer later, once the work and errands are all done.
chat.meaning: Bhai Gurdas pictures the Gursikh rising early, remembering, sitting in the sangat, then working honestly and sharing: remembering first, the work inside it.

Ang.meaning: a page of the Guru Granth Sahib

sangat.meaning: the gathering of the Guru's Sikhs

notes: Bhai Gurdas pauri reference uncertain: the Gursikh who rises in the last watch of the night, bathes, recites/remembers, goes to the sangat and earns honestly appears in several vars (e.g. Var 40 pauri 11; Var 12). Please confirm the best single citation.
Ang 305–306 paraphrased: Guru Ram Das, 'gur satgur ka jo sikh akhae...' (rises early, bathes in the pool of nectar, meditates on the Name, sings the Guru's word through the day). Confirm the Ang.
'Gursikh puts two words together: Gur and Sikh' is a compound, not an etymological claim; confirm phrasing.
howItsDone describes the amrit vela as Sikh custom; confirm phrasing.
